question: Do leave-one-feature-out retraining, permutation importance, accumulated local effects, and SHAP reveal meaningfully different and valid feature-use behavior in simulated VQC and quantum-kernel classifiers than in classical SVC and random-forest baselines on multiclass Iris data?

key_findings.claim: The paper is a small empirical comparison of four classifiers and four explanation tools, not evidence of quantum advantage.
key_findings.evidence: It MinMax-scales the 150-row, four-feature, three-class Iris dataset, uses one nominal 80/20 split, and compares SVC and Random Forest with simulated VQC and QSVC models. It applies leave-one-out retraining, test-set permutation importance, ALE, and KernelSHAP, then explicitly concedes that it has not found a reliable quantum advantage.

key_findings.claim: The headline accuracy ranking is QSVC 0.97, SVC 0.93, Random Forest 0.90, and VQC 0.87 on only 30 nominal test examples.
key_findings.evidence: Table V and the confusion matrices report those four accuracies. Each changed prediction therefore moves accuracy by 3.33 percentage points, and the apparent QSVC lead over SVC is one example. The manuscript nevertheless calls QSVC the superior or preferred model when quantum resources are available.

key_findings.claim: The released artifact strongly indicates that the headline quantum evaluation is contaminated by train-test overlap.
key_findings.evidence: The main notebook loads serialized quantum models and constructs its displayed test set with random_state=470. The only released VQC and QSVC training paths use random_state=4701. Reconstructing both sklearn splits gives 26 of the 30 rows in the headline 470 test set inside the 4701 training set, with only four rows shared with the intended 4701 test set. The QSVC artifact reports 0.8667 on that intended split but the loaded model scores 0.9667 on the headline split; the analogous VQC outputs are 0.80 and 0.8667. Because the pickles have no provenance manifest and current save lines are commented, this is strong evidence conditional on the released training paths, not proof of the binaries' exact lineage.

key_findings.claim: The published test-class counts contradict the confusion matrices and the executable split.
key_findings.evidence: Table III states that the test set contains 7 Setosa, 9 Versicolor, and 14 Virginica examples, while Figure 13 and a direct reconstruction of random_state=470 contain 9, 7, and 14. The prose also says that the classical models correctly classified all seven Versicolor samples while the matrices show seven Versicolor rows but nine Setosa rows. This is a concrete reporting inconsistency in the denominator underlying all class metrics.

key_findings.claim: The bootstrap analysis resamples fixed test predictions and cannot establish training stability, model superiority, or generalization uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: The released code draws 1,000 bootstrap samples from the same 30 held-out label-prediction pairs without refitting any model. Table VI's means therefore reproduce the four point accuracies, and its percentile spreads mainly quantify finite-test-set resampling. Resetting the same random generator for each model permits paired comparisons, but the paper only plots marginal boxes and treats their overlap as evidence that models are suitable for comparison rather than reporting paired differences, confidence intervals, or a test.

key_findings.claim: VQC architecture selection is tuned directly on the test split and exposes substantial run instability.
key_findings.evidence: Sixteen combinations of two optimizers, two ansatz families, and one to four repetitions are scored on the same held-out split, with no validation set, nested resampling, or repeated initialization. Saved notebook output ranges from 0.60 to 0.9333 and runtimes from about 61 to 5,761 seconds. The paper chooses COBYLA plus EfficientSU2 with three repetitions for speed and later reports 0.87, while the saved sweep for that configuration reports 0.80, so a single selected run is not stable enough to support fine accuracy comparisons.

key_findings.claim: The leave-one-out experiment uses a different split from the headline comparison, so its full-feature rows are not the same baselines.
key_findings.evidence: The artifact's LOO notebooks use random_state=4701 rather than 470. Consequently the SVC full-feature score is 0.90 instead of the headline 0.93, and the QSVC full-feature score is 0.87 instead of 0.97. Treating changes in Tables VIII-XI as explanations of the headline models silently crosses experimental populations and, for the loaded quantum models, the same missing provenance problem remains.

key_findings.claim: The leave-one-out results are too coarse and unstable to establish distinct quantum feature-use behavior.
key_findings.evidence: SVC and Random Forest remain at 0.90 or rise to 0.93 after omissions; QSVC stays at 0.87 or rises to 0.90. VQC varies more: 0.87 full, 0.83 without sepal width, 0.93 without petal length, and 0.73 without petal width. These are changes of one to four predictions in a single 30-row split, with no seed distribution, uncertainty, matched retraining budget, or correction for repeated feature tests. The Random Forest omission models are also unseeded in the artifact.

key_findings.claim: Permutation importance broadly recovers the familiar Iris petal-feature ranking for SVC, Random Forest, and QSVC, whereas VQC distributes importance more evenly.
key_findings.evidence: Across 30 shuffles per feature in the released code, petal length and petal width cause the largest accuracy drops for SVC, Random Forest, and QSVC, while the VQC plot assigns material importance to all four features. The paper interprets this as a fundamentally different VQC approach, but no repeated model fits, conditional permutations, group permutations, or null-feature controls test whether it is a reproducible model property rather than seed, split, or estimator noise.

key_findings.claim: Correlation between petal length and petal width defeats a simple causal reading of all three marginal importance methods.
key_findings.evidence: The manuscript itself notes the strong petal-feature correlation and repeatedly observes opposite LOO and permutation directions. With substitutable predictors, drop-column retraining measures the value conditional on the retained feature, marginal permutation creates off-manifold combinations, and KernelSHAP with a marginal background can split credit arbitrarily. No conditional, grouped, or synthetic ground-truth analysis resolves these estimands before the paper attributes disagreement to how quantum models process features.

anchors.section: V.A-B Iris Dataset and Data Preprocessing

key_findings.claim: The ALE comparison is based on only the 30 test rows, omits VQC, and reports sparse descriptive curves without uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: ALE is computed for SVC, Random Forest, and QSVC because the VQC implementation does not expose the required probability vector. The explanation distribution is the single 30-row test split, leaving few observations per interval and class. Figures 24-28 show qualitatively similar petal effects and somewhat larger QSVC sepal effects, but no bin occupancy, interval sensitivity, repeated split, uncertainty band, or quantitative curve distance is reported.

anchors.section: VII.A.3 Accumulated Local Effects Feature Importance

key_findings.claim: The ALE narrative assigns physical centimeters to normalized unitless values.
key_findings.evidence: Section V says every feature is MinMax-scaled to [0,1]. The explanation section nevertheless calls the interval 0.25 to 0.65 centimeters. Those values are scaled coordinates unless explicitly inverse-transformed, and the released ALE path does not perform that inverse transformation. The plots therefore cannot support the physical-unit interpretation as written.

key_findings.claim: The KernelSHAP implementation explains arbitrary numeric class codes rather than class probabilities, invalidating the class-specific interpretation.
key_findings.evidence: The repository calls shap.KernelExplainer(model.predict, test_features), so the scalar explained function returns nominal labels 0, 1, or 2. The waterfalls visibly have base values near 1.1, 1.067, and 1.2 and add contributions toward those encoded integers. Relabeling the same species would change the explanations although model decisions are unchanged. The text then reads positive and negative contributions as evidence for Setosa, Versicolor, or Virginica and even misnames feature 2 as petal width when Table XII identifies it as petal length.

anchors.section: Table XII and SVC, Random Forest, and QSVC SHAP Values

key_findings.claim: No experiment validates whether any explanation is faithful, stable, useful, or correct.
key_findings.evidence: The paper compares visual rankings and narrates one selected misclassified example. It supplies no known-relevant-feature synthetic benchmark, nuisance-feature control, deletion or insertion curve, infidelity or sensitivity metric, rank stability across seeds, resampling confidence interval, counterfactual validity check, human study, or agreement with a mechanistic ground truth. Agreement among LOO, permutation, ALE, and SHAP would not itself be validation because they target different estimands.

anchors.section: Summary of Analysis and IX Conclusion

key_findings.claim: The quantum and classical arms are not controlled well enough to attribute differences to quantum computation.
key_findings.evidence: SVC, Random Forest, VQC, and QSVC have different hypothesis classes, objectives, optimizers, capacities, stochasticity, and tuning budgets. QSVC is a classical support-vector classifier over a kernel matrix produced by an ideal simulated quantum feature map; VQC is a variational circuit optimized by COBYLA. No matched classical kernel, parameter-count control, compute budget, random-feature approximation, learning curve, or circuit ablation isolates a quantum contribution.

anchors.section: III.B.2-3 Variational Quantum Classifier and Quantum Support Vector Machines

key_findings.claim: The experiment says nothing about hardware robustness, finite-shot behavior, runtime advantage, or scaling.
key_findings.evidence: Both quantum models run locally on an ideal simulator. The paper reports that larger VQC configurations take up to roughly one to one-and-a-half hours locally, but supplies no shot count, noise model, hardware queue/runtime, error mitigation, circuit-depth scaling, kernel-estimation error, classical simulation cost curve, or comparison as examples, features, and classes grow. The conclusion correctly identifies the absence of actual quantum-computer training as a major limitation.

key_findings.claim: Several background claims about quantum information are mathematically incorrect or materially misleading.
key_findings.evidence: Page 5 says n classical bits represent n squared states while n qubits can be in 2 to the n states; an n-bit register also has 2 to the n configurations, although a deterministic register occupies one configuration at a time. It calls alpha and beta probabilities even though they are complex amplitudes whose squared magnitudes are probabilities, and says they cannot be measured without noting repeated-preparation tomography. Page 6 writes angle encoding as a sum of R(theta)|0> and R(theta)|1>, which is not a normalized state-preparation definition. Simulator exercises elsewhere are described as demonstrations of quantum advantage even though no comparative resource or learning advantage is measured.

key_findings.claim: The novelty is a narrow combination of off-the-shelf explainers on multiclass Iris, and the related-work comparison omits a directly relevant 2023 visual-analytics system.
key_findings.evidence: The authors claim the first comprehensive multi-class classical-versus-quantum explainability comparison. Their own Table II already lists prior QML feature importance, SHAP, and gate-Shapley work, so the incremental scope is combining four model families and four existing tools on one toy dataset. VIOLET, submitted in December 2023 before this paper, already visualized QNN encoding, ansatz dynamics, and learned features and evaluated usability with case studies and 12 experts, but is absent from the related-work table.

key_findings.claim: The released artifact is useful for forensic inspection but cannot reproduce the reported study cleanly or safely.
key_findings.evidence: The repository contains 11 notebooks, saved figures/CSVs, a small plotting script, and three unversioned serialized Qiskit models, but no tests, CI, lockfile, split manifest, model-provenance manifest, or end-to-end driver. requirements.txt contains mutually exclusive exact pins for Pillow 9.2.0 and 10.2.0 and pyOpenSSL 22.0.0 and 24.0.0 while omitting imported packages including Qiskit Machine Learning, Qiskit Algorithms, SHAP, Alibi, SciPy, and notebook tooling. Two notebooks have source-level syntax errors, two have saved undefined-name failures, execution counts are stateful, and tracked virtual-environment scripts contain a developer-specific path. Loading the remote pickle artifacts would execute untrusted serialization code, so they were inspected structurally rather than executed.

method.core_idea: Train classical SVC and Random Forest baselines plus simulated VQC and QSVC counterparts on normalized Iris data, then compare their predictive results and feature explanations using four established post-hoc methods.
method.mechanism: A ZZFeatureMap encodes four scaled features for VQC and QSVC. VQC combines the feature map with a selected EfficientSU2 ansatz and COBYLA optimization; QSVC uses a FidelityQuantumKernel with compute-uncompute sampling. Leave-one-out retrains after deleting one feature, permutation importance shuffles a held-out feature repeatedly, ALE averages local probability changes over feature intervals, and KernelSHAP approximates feature coalitions around one selected test case. Classical SVC and Random Forest supply reference predictions and explanations.
assumptions: One 80/20 Iris split is representative enough to compare model families and explanations.
Serialized quantum models correspond exactly to the data split and training paths used for headline evaluation.
Accuracy differences of one or a few examples on a 30-row test set are scientifically meaningful.
Test-set scoring can be used both to choose the VQC configuration and to report its performance.
Marginal feature perturbations remain meaningful despite strong petal-feature correlation.
Predicted class integers are a valid scalar target for KernelSHAP and can be interpreted class-wise.
Ideal local simulation is informative about practical quantum behavior.
Differences among unmatched SVC, Random Forest, VQC, and QSVC models can illuminate quantum-specific feature use.
Explanation plots can be assessed by visual plausibility without a ground-truth or fidelity benchmark.

techniques.role: Map all four Iris features into [0,1] before classical training and quantum feature encoding.
Provide the principal classical kernel-classification baseline.
Provide a nonlinear tree-ensemble baseline with a different inductive bias.
Combine ZZFeatureMap, EfficientSU2, and COBYLA in a simulated variational quantum classifier.
Fit a support-vector classifier using a simulated fidelity quantum kernel.
Retrain each model after deleting one feature and compare held-out accuracy.
Shuffle one held-out feature repeatedly and measure the accuracy decrease.
Estimate global and class-specific accumulated local probability effects for SVC, Random Forest, and QSVC.
Approximate local contributions for a selected test case, although the artifact incorrectly targets scalar class labels.
Resample fixed held-out prediction pairs 1,000 times to display accuracy distributions without refitting.

evaluations.setting: Headline classification on a single 30-row Iris test split (PDF pp. 10-15)
evaluations.metric: Accuracy, per-class precision/recall/F1, and confusion matrices
evaluations.result: QSVC 0.97, SVC 0.93, Random Forest 0.90, and VQC 0.87; the QSVC-SVC gap is one prediction.
evaluations.baseline: Four unmatched model families on the same nominal random_state=470 split; no repeated seeds or uncertainty.

evaluations.setting: Released split-lineage reconstruction for the loaded quantum models (artifact audit; manuscript pp. 9-15 and repository link p. 23)
evaluations.metric: Row-index overlap between the headline random_state=470 test set and released random_state=4701 quantum-training split
evaluations.result: 26 of 30 headline test rows fall in the apparent released training set; only four overlap the released intended test set. The inference is conditional because model pickle provenance is absent.
evaluations.baseline: Exact sklearn split reconstruction and the only released VQC/QSVC training notebooks.

evaluations.setting: Fixed-prediction bootstrap on the same 30 test pairs (PDF pp. 12-13)
evaluations.metric: Mean and interquartile range of 1,000 resampled accuracies
evaluations.result: Means are 0.932233 SVC, 0.965567 QSVC, 0.900333 Random Forest, and 0.864833 VQC; distributions overlap.
evaluations.baseline: No refitting, no new split, no paired-difference analysis, and no training-seed variability.

evaluations.setting: VQC hyperparameter sweep on one split (PDF pp. 9-12)
evaluations.metric: Held-out accuracy and elapsed runtime across 16 optimizer/ansatz/repetition combinations
evaluations.result: Saved scores span 0.60-0.9333 and runtimes about 61-5,761 seconds; the chosen COBYLA/EfficientSU2/reps=3 configuration has a saved sweep score of 0.80 but later appears at 0.87.
evaluations.baseline: Two optimizers, two ansätze, and repetitions 1-4, all selected on the test set without a validation split.

evaluations.setting: SVC and Random Forest leave-one-feature-out retraining (PDF pp. 14-15)
evaluations.metric: Accuracy after dropping each of four features
evaluations.result: SVC is 0.90 full and 0.93 without either petal feature; Random Forest is 0.90 full and 0.93 without petal length, with other omissions at 0.90.
evaluations.baseline: Different random_state=4701 split from the headline results; the Random Forest omission fits are unseeded.

evaluations.setting: VQC and QSVC leave-one-feature-out retraining (PDF pp. 16-18)
evaluations.result: VQC changes from 0.87 full to 0.87/0.83/0.93/0.73; QSVC changes from 0.87 to 0.90/0.87/0.90/0.87 in sepal-length, sepal-width, petal-length, petal-width order.
evaluations.baseline: Single split and apparent single fits; quantum artifact lineage is not documented.

evaluations.setting: Permutation importance on the held-out rows (PDF pp. 17-20)
evaluations.result: SVC, Random Forest, and QSVC emphasize petal length and width; VQC shows a flatter four-feature profile with broad whiskers.
evaluations.baseline: Marginal shuffling without grouped/conditional permutations, nuisance controls, or model-refit variability.

evaluations.metric: Magnitude and shape of accumulated local probability effects
evaluations.result: SVC and QSVC are qualitatively similar, with QSVC showing greater effect magnitude for three of four features, especially petal length; VQC is omitted.
evaluations.baseline: Only 30 explanation rows, unknown bin occupancy, no curve-distance metric or uncertainty.

evaluations.setting: Class-specific ALE for Versicolor and Virginica (PDF pp. 18-22)
evaluations.metric: Feature-value versus class-probability ALE curves for SVC, Random Forest, and QSVC
evaluations.result: Petal effects switch direction between Versicolor and Virginica, while QSVC shows larger sepal effects in the displayed curves.
evaluations.baseline: Descriptive plots on scaled values; the manuscript mistakenly labels normalized positions as centimeters.

evaluations.setting: KernelSHAP explanation of selected test point 4 (PDF pp. 19-22)
evaluations.metric: Waterfall contributions for SVC, Random Forest, and QSVC
evaluations.result: The narrative attributes the correct QSVC prediction to petal features and contrasts it with two incorrect classical predictions.
evaluations.baseline: Explains model.predict integer labels with the test set as background, so the additive target is an arbitrary class code rather than a class probability.

evaluations.setting: Official code and result artifact audit (PDF Table I pp. 3-4; repository link p. 23)
evaluations.metric: Static executability, dependency consistency, result lineage, and reproduction completeness
evaluations.result: Classical matrices reproduce, but the repository has contradictory pins, missing dependencies, two syntactically invalid notebooks, saved undefined-name errors, stateful outputs, unsafe unversioned model pickles, and no end-to-end reproducibility or provenance controls.
evaluations.baseline: All 11 notebooks, the plotting script, README, requirements, saved CSVs/images, and model metadata at official repository HEAD 7b1a50bef26eaed77d8db2d4ea1fecf33ab1ce3d.

limitations: The dataset has only 150 rows, four features, and three balanced classes and is a teaching benchmark rather than a demanding QML workload.
Only one nominal 80/20 split is used, so results do not estimate split or training-seed variability.
The headline test set contains only 30 rows; each prediction changes accuracy by 3.33 percentage points.
Released model-training paths and headline evaluation use different random seeds, producing apparent overlap of 26 test rows with quantum training data.
Serialized quantum models have no provenance manifest, preventing definitive reconstruction of which code, split, dependency versions, and parameters produced them.
VQC configurations are selected directly on the same held-out split later used for reporting.
The VQC sweep does not repeat stochastic initialization, so a selected configuration's variance is unknown.
The paper's reported test-class counts contradict its confusion matrices and executable split.
Leave-one-out analysis uses a different split from the headline evaluation while being narrated as though it explains the same models.
Random Forest leave-one-out models are unseeded in the released artifact.
The bootstrap resamples fixed predictions rather than retraining models or resampling the full learning procedure.
No paired bootstrap differences, confidence intervals for model gaps, hypothesis tests, or multiple-comparison adjustments are reported.
Permutation importance uses only 30 shuffles and does not quantify estimator or fit variability.
Marginal shuffling and SHAP backgrounds ignore strong petal-feature correlation and can create off-manifold inputs.
ALE is estimated on only 30 held-out rows, with no bin counts, interval sensitivity, or uncertainty bands.
VQC is omitted from ALE because the selected interface does not provide the required probability vector.
KernelSHAP explains integer class labels instead of per-class probabilities or decision scores.
The test set is reused as the SHAP background and the pool from which the displayed example is chosen.
Only one selected local example is narrated; there is no representative or pre-registered case set.
No explanation-fidelity, stability, sparsity, ground-truth recovery, counterfactual, or human-usefulness metric is evaluated.
Classical and quantum models are unmatched in hypothesis class, capacity, optimization, tuning budget, and runtime.
No classical approximation to the quantum kernel or matched random-feature/kernel baseline is included.
Both quantum models use ideal local simulation; no finite-shot, noise, hardware, or mitigation experiment is run.
No learning curve, feature-count scaling, class-count scaling, circuit-depth scaling, or wall-clock/energy cost curve is reported.
Several quantum-computing explanations and the angle-encoding equation are mathematically incorrect or misleading.
The official repository lacks tests, CI, a consistent installable environment, an end-to-end runner, split manifests, and result provenance.
Unversioned pickle artifacts are unsafe to load and are not a durable or auditable model-exchange format.
The paper's broad novelty framing overlooks VIOLET and reduces a diverse XQAI literature to a feature checklist.
failure_modes: A serialized quantum model trained on the 4701 training split is evaluated on the 470 test split, leaking most evaluation rows and inflating apparent accuracy.
A different undocumented binary provenance makes the leakage inference false while still leaving the result irreproducible.
Test-set hyperparameter search selects a lucky VQC initialization or architecture and produces optimistic performance.
One misclassified Iris row reverses the ranking of two models or the sign of a feature-omission effect.
Correlated petal features substitute for one another under deletion but become unrealistic combinations under marginal permutation.
Unseeded Random Forest retraining is mistaken for a deterministic feature-removal effect.
Fixed-prediction bootstrapping is mistaken for evidence of training stability or deployment generalization.
KernelSHAP contributions change when class codes are permuted even though the classifier is identical.
Sparse ALE intervals on 30 rows create visually dramatic bends that disappear under another split or binning scheme.
A visually plausible explanation is treated as faithful without perturbation, consistency, or known-ground-truth validation.
Differences caused by model capacity, optimization, or stochastic initialization are labeled quantum-specific behavior.
Ideal statevector behavior fails under finite shots, device noise, transpilation, and calibration drift.
A small simulator result is extrapolated to more features even though quantum-kernel estimation and variational training costs grow sharply.
Conflicting exact dependency pins prevent installation, while stale notebook outputs conceal current syntax or name errors.
Executing an untrusted Qiskit pickle compromises the environment or silently depends on incompatible library internals.
reusable_insights: Treat dataset split identity as first-class provenance: store row IDs, split hashes, seeds, preprocessing state, and the exact split used to train every serialized model.
Never tune on the final test set; use nested validation and lock the test set before explanation analysis.
For a 30-row test set, report exact paired predictions and paired uncertainty rather than decimals that imply unsupported precision.
Separate uncertainty from test sampling, split choice, training initialization, shot noise, and device noise instead of calling one fixed-prediction bootstrap stability.
Validate explanations on synthetic tasks with known relevant and nuisance features before interpreting disagreements on correlated real features.
Use grouped or conditional perturbations when features are correlated, and state the estimand of deletion, permutation, ALE, and SHAP separately.
For multiclass SHAP, explain per-class probabilities or decision scores and test invariance to class-label renaming.
Quantify explanation fidelity and stability with deletion/insertion, infidelity, sensitivity, rank correlation, seed intervals, and counterfactual checks.
Match classical and quantum baselines by representation, capacity, tuning budget, and compute; include a classical approximation to any simulated quantum kernel.
Evaluate a ladder from exact simulator to finite shots, calibrated noise, and hardware, with circuit and error budgets reported at every rung.
Measure scaling directly across sample count, feature count, class count, circuit depth, shots, and wall-clock cost rather than claiming that a small run will extrapolate.
Use safe, versioned model formats or reproducible training scripts instead of distributing opaque pickle binaries.

A useful XQAI study should distinguish prediction explanation, circuit-component explanation, hardware-failure explanation, and ante-hoc interpretability rather than collapse them into one feature-ranking task.
open_questions: Does the headline QSVC result survive when every model is retrained from scratch on one committed split with a sealed test set?
How large are accuracy and explanation-rank distributions over repeated splits, initialization seeds, and VQC optimizer restarts?
Can an exact manifest establish the lineage of the three released serialized quantum models?
Do QSVC and a matched classical kernel or random Fourier feature model differ after equal tuning and compute budgets?
Which apparent VQC feature differences remain after controlling ansatz, initialization, training convergence, and model capacity?
How do grouped and conditional permutation, conditional SHAP, and correlation-preserving deletion change the Iris rankings?
Can a synthetic multiclass benchmark with known causal, redundant, nuisance, and interaction features recover ground-truth explanations for VQC and QSVC?
Are local explanations invariant to class-label permutation when per-class scores replace integer predictions?
How many samples per ALE interval are required for stable quantum/classical curve comparisons, and how should uncertainty be displayed?
Do explanation rankings survive finite-shot sampling, calibrated noise models, different transpilation seeds, and actual hardware drift?
What is the end-to-end break-even point, including kernel construction, optimizer evaluations, simulation, hardware queue time, and classical baselines?
How do feature importance and explanation fidelity scale with 8, 16, or more features when exact simulation becomes costly?
Can circuit-native gate or component explanations predict failures that input-feature attribution misses?
Would users make better debugging or scientific decisions with these explanations in a realistic domain rather than Iris?
Which claims remain after an independent, clean-environment reproduction that executes every notebook in order and regenerates every table and figure?

competitive_landscape.title: Study of Feature Importance for Quantum Machine Learning Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: The direct predecessor compares VQC and QSVC feature importance with classical counterparts using permutation importance and ALE on real ESPN fantasy-football data.
competitive_landscape.difference: It additionally evaluates IBM hardware and introduces tiering, aggregation, validation, and diversity analysis; the target adds LOO, multiclass Iris, and local SHAP but is smaller and simulator-only.

competitive_landscape.title: eXplainable AI for Quantum Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: An earlier QML-XAI study applies Baseline SHAP and Integrated Gradients to parametrized quantum circuits and analyzes quantum-specific computation constraints.
competitive_landscape.difference: It focuses on shot-induced convergence and exponential circuit phase space rather than a classical-versus-quantum Iris checklist, giving it a more explicit quantum explanation-complexity analysis.

competitive_landscape.title: Explaining Quantum Circuits with Shapley Values: Towards Explainable Quantum Machine Learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A quantum-native Shapley framework attributes goals to individual gates or gate groups across classification, generation, transpilation, and optimization.
competitive_landscape.difference: It explains circuit structure on simulators and two superconducting devices, whereas the target applies classical input-feature SHAP to model.predict labels on an ideal simulator.

competitive_landscape.title: Explainable quantum regression algorithm with encoded data structure
competitive_landscape.relationship: An ante-hoc alternative makes variational parameters correspond directly to regression coefficients through a structured data encoding.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its interpretability is architectural and parameter-semantic rather than post-hoc feature attribution; it addresses regression and compressed encoding rather than multiclass Iris classification.

competitive_landscape.title: VIOLET: Visual Analytics for Explainable Quantum Neural Networks
competitive_landscape.relationship: A pre-target visual-analytics system explains QNN encoders, ansatz-state evolution, and learned features through coordinated views.
competitive_landscape.difference: VIOLET adds purpose-designed satellite and augmented-heatmap views, two case studies, and interviews with 12 experts; the target provides static off-the-shelf plots and no user evaluation.

competitive_landscape.title: Opportunities and limitations of explaining quantum machine learning
competitive_landscape.relationship: A post-target field framework introduces Taylor-infinity and quantum layer-wise relevance propagation and evaluates QML explanations against known feature relevance.
competitive_landscape.difference: It uses a controlled six-dimensional four-class synthetic task, explanation-alignment metrics, and finite-shot/storage analysis; the target lacks ground truth, explanation metrics, and quantum-specific methods.

competitive_landscape.title: Explainable Quantum Machine Learning for Multispectral Images Segmentation: Case Study
competitive_landscape.relationship: A real-device XQML case study proposes metrics to explain why hybrid model performance changes on public quantum hardware.
competitive_landscape.difference: It treats hardware behavior and monetary cost as explanation targets in a realistic segmentation task, whereas the target studies only ideal-simulator input attribution on Iris.

competitive_landscape.title: QuXAI: Explainers for Hybrid Quantum Machine Learning Models
competitive_landscape.relationship: QuXAI's Q-MEDLEY combines drop-column and permutation evidence for hybrid quantum-classical feature explanations.
competitive_landscape.difference: It evaluates ten models on noisy Iris and Wine variants with synthetic nuisance features, Recall@3, Spearman rank agreement, component ablations, and open code, directly supplying validation missing from the target.

competitive_landscape.title: Component Based Quantum Machine Learning Explainability
competitive_landscape.relationship: A direct conceptual follow-on decomposes QML explanation into feature maps, ansätze, optimizers, kernels, and quantum-classical loops.
competitive_landscape.difference: It argues for modular component-level ALE, SHAP, spectral, and fidelity analyses instead of the target's monolithic input-output comparison, although its evaluation remains preliminary.

competitive_landscape.title: Towards Explainable Quantum AI: Informing the Encoder Selection of Quantum Neural Networks via Visualization
competitive_landscape.relationship: XQAI-Eyes visualizes how candidate encoders preserve classical patterns and separate class-conditioned quantum states before training.
competitive_landscape.difference: It spans multiple datasets and encoder designs and derives encoder-selection practices with domain experts; the target fixes ZZFeatureMap and explains only post-training predictions.

competitive_landscape.title: Explainable quantum neural networks for multi-material topology optimization
competitive_landscape.relationship: An application-specific QNN maps qubit-wise observables to material decisions and links them to load paths, regions, and interfaces.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its auditable variables are mechanics-facing and tested under boundary-condition, mesh, and 3D transfer; the target offers post-hoc attribution on a fixed toy distribution.

competitive_landscape.title: Do emulated quantum circuits change what CNNs look at? Performance and explainability comparison in medical image classification
competitive_landscape.relationship: A parameter-matched classical-versus-hybrid medical-image study explicitly compares what the two models attend to using SHAP-derived overlap and transport metrics.
competitive_landscape.difference: It varies data and hyperparameters across two real datasets, controls parameters, and finds no consistent dominance; the target has one tiny split, unmatched models, and qualitative plots.

competitive_landscape.title: Explainable quantum-compressed machine learning for complex fluid flows
competitive_landscape.relationship: A structured quantum-compressed surrogate assigns eight circuit parameters to modal frequencies and inter-mode interactions in fluid dynamics.
competitive_landscape.difference: It pursues ante-hoc physical parameter semantics and long-horizon stability on two cardiovascular benchmarks rather than post-hoc Iris feature rankings.

competitive_landscape.title: Benchmarking Quantum Machine Learning for Power-System Attack Detection: Evaluation Choices Decide the Outcome Before the Models Do
competitive_landscape.relationship: A seeded QML benchmark shows that split, tuning, surrogate, and attack choices can reverse conclusions at fixed models.
competitive_landscape.difference: It provides positive controls, matched-dimensionality regimes, adversarial tests, and file-held-out evaluation and finds the quantum arm near chance in the capped regime; it directly illustrates why the target's undocumented split mismatch is outcome-determining.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The work is the first comprehensive direct comparison of classical and quantum machine-learning explainability on multiclass data, extending prior QML feature-importance studies with SVC, Random Forest, VQC, QSVC, leave-one-out, permutation importance, ALE, and SHAP on Iris.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The exact paper does assemble four model families and four established explanation methods into one 23-page worked example, and its visual results document how the selected VQC differs from the other three models in this run. However, the headline quantum evaluation is likely contaminated by a 26-of-30 split overlap, the VQC is tuned on the test set, LOO changes the split, SHAP explains integer labels, ALE is sparse and omits VQC, no explanation is validated, all quantum execution is ideal simulation, and artifact provenance is incomplete. Prior work already covered QML permutation/ALE, PQC SHAP/Integrated Gradients, gate Shapley values, and VIOLET's encoder/ansatz/feature visual analytics.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The narrow pedagogical combination may be locally novel, but the paper does not establish a reliable scientific difference in quantum feature use or a quantum advantage. Its most valuable reuse is as a compact map of common XQAI evaluation failures: split leakage, test-set tuning, fixed-prediction bootstrap, correlated-feature estimand confusion, scalar-label SHAP, sparse ALE, unmatched model families, simulator-only claims, and non-reproducible serialized artifacts. A publishable continuation should begin with immutable data/model lineage, nested repeated training, matched classical kernels, synthetic explanation ground truth, class-score attribution, conditional perturbations, and a simulator-shot-noise-hardware ladder, then ask whether any explanation difference is stable, faithful, useful, and worth its full compute cost.

reviewer_notes: Audited all 23 pages of the exact arXiv v1 PDF, including every table, equation, caption, figure, confusion matrix, feature-importance panel, ALE curve, and SHAP waterfall. Rendered all pages to images, inspected a full contact sheet, and reopened pages 5, 15, and 18-22 at original detail to check the quantum background, test denominators, LOO sign convention, permutation whiskers, ALE units, and SHAP base values. The Figure 13 matrices visibly have class supports 9/7/14, contradicting Table III's 7/9/14. Audited the official repository https://github.com/LukePower01/ml-to-qml at HEAD 7b1a50bef26eaed77d8db2d4ea1fecf33ab1ce3d (2024-12-14) using the official codeload archive, SHA-256 6cccb5f0df2910d019639ae3f05b1b1453441fe8c26239876912e7547d12d467. Read the README, requirements, all 11 notebooks, the Python plotting script, saved CSVs/images, and serialized-model metadata; performed JSON parsing, notebook code extraction, static source/AST checks, CSV/result reconciliation, and Python compilation where possible. Did not execute the three untrusted pickle models or attempt a full rerun in the contradictory and incomplete environment. Reconstructed both sklearn splits, found 26/30 headline rows in the only released quantum-training split, reproduced the classical random_state=470 matrices and accuracies with current sklearn, and compared the released 4701 quantum scores with the loaded-model headline outputs. Competitor research checked current official arXiv primary records through 2026-08-23, including direct predecessors, omitted contemporaneous work, quantum-native and ante-hoc alternatives, explanation-validation follow-ons, component methods, hardware explanation, controlled classical-versus-hybrid comparisons, and a seeded benchmark showing that evaluation choices reverse QML conclusions.
